title: Couch Creatures
user: A parent, older sibling, or two children sharing one laptop/TV who want a gentle cooperative game that starts instantly and does not need accounts, purchases, or separate controllers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A father looking for remote co-op with his 10-year-old describes mobile choices as a 'wasteland of dark patterns, data harvesting, exorbitant recurring fees' after hours of searching.
A 78-score, 66-comment request asks for fun games for two 13-year-olds on one computer; the poster then has to work out what controllers local multiplayer needs.

recurrence: Two independent family/local-play requests in 2025–2026; the second drew 66 comments, and both emphasize access and sane pricing over depth.
current_workaround: Install Steam games, buy or map controllers, sift through mobile free-to-play titles, or give up when coordination games become too chaotic.
incumbents_and_gap: Overcooked, Moving Out, It Takes Two, and Jackbox offer parts of the experience, but require installs, purchases, controllers, or escalation into pressure. There is little no-account web co-op designed for one shared keyboard plus optional phones.
smallest_useful_product: A 2–4 player, 8–12 minute shared-screen rescue game: players use two-key keyboard lanes or scan a local QR to use one-thumb phone controls, herd shy creatures through three changing habitats, and finish with a group postcard. Each run shuffles creature traits, weather, and route hazards. Non-goals: chat, user accounts, endless progression, ads, and competitive matchmaking.
success_measure: At least 35% of started rooms finish two runs and at least 20% use both available input modes in a four-week public test.
monetization: free — the trust proposition is a family-safe, no-account link; a one-time optional cosmetic pack can be evaluated only after repeat play.
constraints: Keyboard accessibility and touch targets must work without permissions; store no child data; avoid voice, chat, ads, and behavioral tracking; WebRTC is not required for same-screen play.
why_distinct: It is cooperative local play deliberately designed around the devices people already have, not a controller-dependent party-game collection.

title: Pause Garden
user: Two to four remote friends with interrupted evenings—especially parents—who want a cozy cooperative game that remains meaningful when someone steps away.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 115-score discussion explicitly asks for more online co-op games to offer a server pause because real-life interruptions make time-sensitive co-op frustrating.
A request for a virtual 2–4 player cozy game specifies older hardware, short sessions, affordability, controller compatibility, and being able to walk away for children without dying.

recurrence: Two high-engagement requests frame interruption tolerance as a core co-op need rather than a minor accessibility setting (115/19 and 108/76 score/comments).
current_workaround: Pick turn-based games, ask friends to wait in voice chat, accept lost progress, or avoid co-op on nights with care duties.
incumbents_and_gap: Stardew Valley offers a pause model in some contexts; real-time co-op games such as Peak and many farming games do not. Existing cozy games are usually built around continuous presence rather than graceful handoff.
smallest_useful_product: A 2–4 player room-code garden-restoration game. In 15-minute chapters, each player places one action token at a time; an absent player becomes a harmless 'sleeping sprite' whose queued token can be completed by the group. Runs vary by weather, seed goals, and visitor requests. Non-goals: real-time combat, timers that punish absence, persistent grind, and social feed features.
success_measure: In beta, 50% of rooms use the pause/away flow at least once and 70% of those rooms complete their chapter rather than abandoning it.
monetization: one-time — a small finished cooperative game fits an upfront host unlock better than subscriptions or retention mechanics.
constraints: Room state needs durable, privacy-minimal server storage and reconnect handling; no account should be needed; game must remain playable on older integrated GPUs and with keyboard-only input.
why_distinct: The away-player mechanic is part of the game’s cooperative strategy, rather than an afterthought pause button on a real-time clone.

title: Hand of Two
user: Couples and friends who want a quick, replayable two-player tactical card game without buying a collectible deck or learning a 40-minute ruleset.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster asks for favorite two-person card games after enjoying German Whist and Cribbage with their spouse.
A 151-score, 75-comment co-op request seeks games for two or more people that are actually fun with little to no internet, specifically to prepare in advance.

recurrence: Separate two-player and low-connectivity threads, with 75 responses in the latter, show a recurring desire for compact social play outside a large online service.
current_workaround: Learn traditional card games, buy a physical deck, install a multiplayer client, or send links to heavyweight digital card games.
incumbents_and_gap: Cribbage, German Whist, Cuttle, and Board Game Arena offer card play, but are either physical, need accounts/large rulesets, or present a broad platform rather than an immediate 12-minute duel.
smallest_useful_product: A room-code, two-player browser card duel with a fixed 18-card shared deck. Players draft three weather cards, play six simultaneous turns to protect or disrupt a tiny expedition, and reveal a short story epilogue. Each run changes the card mix and map modifier. Inputs are mouse/touch; a game takes 10–15 minutes. Non-goals: collectible cards, ranked ladder, purchases of power, and spectator chat.
success_measure: At least 30% of first rooms immediately start a rematch and median completed match time stays between 8 and 16 minutes.
monetization: one-time — a complete tactical deck and future scenario packs are legible purchases without turning the game into a CCG.
constraints: Use server-authoritative simultaneous resolution to prevent easy room-code cheating; support reconnect within one turn; all art and text must be original and avoid trading-card IP.
why_distinct: It is a finite, original micro-duel about shared prediction, not a browser port of an established card game or a collectible economy.

title: Aisle 47
user: Small groups travelling or gathering in weak-connectivity settings who want a three-to-six player bluffing game that can be joined from a link and end before boarding or dinner.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer recreating in-flight poker and Liar's Dice says the missing social play motivated BLE games with no Internet access, analytics, or tracking, and asks what other games people want.
A 268-score, 72-comment maintained list asks for genuinely fun free games with no ads, IAPs, gacha, or predatory mechanics; its criteria explicitly reject those workarounds.

recurrence: One thread identifies lost local social play in travel; another large community thread explicitly filters out the monetization patterns that dominate mobile casual games.
current_workaround: Install separate apps before meeting, use a physical bluffing game, depend on Bluetooth-specific apps, or tolerate ads and data collection.
incumbents_and_gap: Airplane-mode poker/Liar's Dice, Spaceteam, and Jackbox prove demand for device-mediated groups, but have app, purchase, host, or setup friction. A web-first option needs a light transport and a full ending.
smallest_useful_product: A three-to-six player browser bluffing game in which each phone receives a hidden cargo manifest and the shared screen shows a train aisle. Players make six timed-but-pausable inspections, then vote on the smuggler; a whole game takes 12 minutes. A host can cache the game as a PWA before travel and create a six-character room code. Non-goals: gambling, real-money stakes, account login, ads, and endless lobbies.
success_measure: At least 25% of cached/offline-capable host sessions successfully connect four or more players and complete a second round in field testing.
monetization: one-time — a party host can buy optional scenario packs; no ads or player-data business model is compatible with the evidence.
constraints: Offline discovery must have a fallback QR/manual code path because Web Bluetooth and local-network support differ across iOS and Android; never collect device contacts or precise location.
why_distinct: It is a deliberately finite, privacy-respecting travel party game, not a gambling simulation or another large party-game platform.

title: Rulebook Relay
user: Daily-puzzle regulars bored of word clones who want one mobile-friendly browser puzzle with a fresh but learnable rule twist each day.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster explicitly asks whether there is a daily puzzle where the rules change every day and whether there would be interest.
A federated repost of Gerrymandle describes a daily puzzle where players redraw electoral districts, showing appetite for a daily format with a non-word core mechanic.

recurrence: The explicit 'rules change every day' request is reinforced by a current daily game built around a distinctive systemic mechanic rather than another word grid.
current_workaround: Maintain a bookmark folder of many daily games, accept repeating mechanics, or play one-off puzzle archives.
incumbents_and_gap: Wordle, Connections, Puzzmo, and numerous -dles deliver routine, while daily experimental games can be opaque. There is room for a predictable learning scaffold around rotating rules.
smallest_useful_product: A one-screen daily logistics puzzle: slide three couriers across a 6×6 board in under 40 moves while one printed 'rule card' changes (mirrors, shared fuel, one-way bridges, etc.). A 30-second interactive example teaches that day's mutation; a six-day week ends with a remix. Inputs are tap/drag or arrows; each attempt is 3–8 minutes. Non-goals: word lists, AI-generated riddles, streak penalties, and social posting gates.
success_measure: At least 40% of day-one players return for three distinct rule cards in the first week, while tutorial abandonment remains under 20%.
monetization: free — a daily link should have zero first-run friction; a one-time archive/supporter unlock may follow only if it does not fragment the daily puzzle.
constraints: Every daily seed must be solvable and independently verified; avoid real election content or political targeting despite the cited genre example; cache puzzles and store streaks locally by default.
why_distinct: The product is a carefully authored rule-language and teaching pattern, not an automated stream of generic daily puzzles.

title: Dawn Run
user: People who already play a free daily web game and want a short, non-word, same-seed roguelike run they can compare without committing to a live-service RPG.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user asks for more daily games specifically requiring free play, browser access rather than an app, and a new puzzle every day after tiring of Wordle.
A current post highlights Rogule: a minimalist online browser roguelike where everyone receives the same dungeon each day and gets one chance to beat it.

recurrence: The request specifies a browser-based daily habit, while the Rogule discussion validates the same-dungeon daily-run pattern in the open web.
current_workaround: Play word puzzles, install a roguelike, or use a daily game whose session is either too long or too unforgiving to share casually.
incumbents_and_gap: Rogule demonstrates the seed-and-one-chance concept; traditional roguelikes and Vampire Survivors-style games target longer, more combat-heavy sessions. The gap is an approachable 5–7 minute tactical run with a readable post-run comparison.
smallest_useful_product: A daily browser roguelike of exactly six rooms. Pick one of three tools, route through visible hazards, and decide when to cash out before a final chase; everyone gets the same seed but different offered tools. Tap/click or arrow keys; runs take 5–7 minutes. Non-goals: procedural endless mode, gacha classes, energy timers, and real-time PvP.
success_measure: At least 30% of daily starters submit a completed score and at least 20% return on three separate days during the first two weeks.
monetization: free — daily comparison only works when the seed is universally accessible; optional one-time cosmetic trails must not alter choices.
constraints: Publish deterministic seeds and replay data for leaderboard verification; limit pseudonymous score retention; ensure the daily can be completed with keyboard, touch, and reduced motion.
why_distinct: It compresses the roguelike decision arc into a finished daily micro-run rather than imitating a large dungeon crawler.

title: Rankless Rally
user: Puzzle players who enjoy improving a score but do not want a grindy ranked ladder, account requirement, or a daily puzzle that disappears forever.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A creator reports that a simple daily leaderboard caused active players to replay logic puzzles to improve rank more than progression did, despite no rewards or sharing incentives.
A post about enclose.horse praises a one-a-day spatial puzzle that also permits the whole archive and user-made levels, rather than locking play behind a single daily board.

recurrence: One source observes score-driven replay directly; the other highlights that a daily format can coexist with an accessible archive and creation.
current_workaround: Replay the daily until it is optimized, keep screenshots of old scores, or move to a competitive game with a full ranking system.
incumbents_and_gap: Daily leaderboards and Puzzmo-style archives exist, but standard rank tables intensify competition. Casual players lack a compact score game that celebrates personal improvement and lets a host share a replay without an account.
smallest_useful_product: A 90-second spatial-routing puzzle with one daily board and a permanent archive. Each board awards a three-part 'rally card'—speed, elegance, and rescue count—so players can improve different dimensions; a replay ghost shows only a chosen friend’s path via a room code. Inputs are mouse/touch/keyboard. Non-goals: global MMR, chat, streak loss, algorithmic feed, and user-generated content moderation in v1.
success_measure: At least 25% of completed boards are replayed once and at least 15% of players open a shared replay ghost without creating an account.
monetization: free — the score card and archive must remain shareable; a one-time theme pack can support hosting without selling retries.
constraints: Anti-cheat should verify deterministic move logs server-side; do not expose personal profiles by default; provide color-blind-safe route symbols.
why_distinct: It treats improvement as several interpretable personal goals, not as an engagement ladder or a clone of an existing daily puzzle.

title: Puzzle Late
user: Daily-puzzle fans who finish a puzzle quickly and want more original, browser-native challenges available immediately without copying a newspaper game’s archive.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Connections fan says that after finishing the daily puzzle 'that's it until tomorrow' and built a replay archive with optional hints to solve that limitation.
An itch.io discussion argues for a true browser experience with 'no install, no account, just a tab'; replies also expose the need to budget for low-memory machines.

recurrence: One player-facing thread documents the post-daily shortage; a separate browser-distribution discussion reinforces that immediate play and broad device support are valuable but require discipline.
current_workaround: Replay a proprietary game through unofficial archives, wait until tomorrow, install a puzzle app, or browse a large unsorted puzzle site.
incumbents_and_gap: NYT Games and Puzzmo create daily habits, while archive sites often depend on another publisher’s content. The unresolved gap is a fully original, small puzzle anthology that is intentionally playable after the daily is done.
smallest_useful_product: A zero-account browser anthology of 40 original 'late puzzles': each is a five-minute visual deduction about timing, shadows, or routes, with two optional non-spoiler nudges and a daily featured shelf. A completed run unlocks a tiny hand-drawn ending card; puzzle order adapts only locally. Non-goals: reproducing any newspaper puzzle, scraped archives, user chat, or 3D assets.
success_measure: At least 45% of visitors complete two different puzzles in one session and fewer than 10% leave before opening a puzzle on a low-end mobile performance test.
monetization: one-time — a complete original anthology has a clear paid value while the first five puzzles can remain free and ad-free.
constraints: All puzzles, wording, and visual language must be original; no use of NYT or other publisher content; keep asset budget below a modest mobile page-load target and preserve accessibility labels.
why_distinct: It solves the after-daily moment with original authored micro-puzzles rather than an unauthorized replay site or generic puzzle generator.

title: Gate Shift
user: Players seeking a tactile, original, browser-friendly logic puzzle with a satisfying finite run rather than a familiar word, merge, or match-three loop.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A detailed beta request presents a new grid slider in which rotating rows and columns through fixed gates creates, changes, or removes tiles, with scoring based on empty space and moves left.
A 2026 itch.io browser-game release frames a small original interaction—bouncing bullets and territory control—as immediately playable in the browser rather than an install.

recurrence: The first thread is a concrete request for feedback on a nonstandard grid mechanic; the second shows indie creators are still bringing compact, mechanic-led games to the browser in 2026.
current_workaround: Play polished but repetitive word/merge games, download an experimental mobile beta, or use puzzle apps that blend finite boards into endless retention loops.
incumbents_and_gap: Threes/2048, sliding blocks, and match games own familiar operations, but they rarely give a short authored campaign with reversible state and an explicit finish. Existing puzzle apps also commonly put experimental games behind an install.
smallest_useful_product: A browser puzzle about rotating six conveyor rings through fixed color gates. A level takes 4–10 minutes and ends after a fixed move budget; every rotation can be previewed, but choosing a shortcut changes future gate polarity. Each run draws one of three deterministic board layouts and a daily challenge. Inputs: swipe, arrows, undo. Non-goals: procedurally infinite boards, match-three monetization, copied mechanics/art, and social ranking in v1.
success_measure: At least 50% of players finish the tutorial board, 25% complete three boards, and the median session reaches a deliberate level ending rather than a quit.
monetization: one-time — a finite set of authored puzzles is a cleaner fit than ads or move sales.
constraints: Puzzle generator must prove target levels solvable; offer undo without penalty; respect reduced-motion settings and make color nonessential through symbols.
why_distinct: The interesting unit is reversible gate-state planning with a hard ending, not another tile-merging or generic slider clone.

title: Orderly Chaos
user: Puzzle-curious adults and teens who enjoy deduction but want a quick visual logic game that teaches itself through play instead of a dense abstract-rules tutorial.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster proposes a puzzle where players turn a partially known order into a total order with minimal comparisons, and explicitly asks whether it would be fun, challenging, or educational.
An itch.io browser release demonstrates current interest in small, social, browser-native interactions rather than requiring a native-client workflow.

recurrence: A concrete request tests an underused deduction mechanic, while a separate 2026 browser release supports a low-friction experimental-web format.
current_workaround: Use logic-grid puzzle books, play number-sorting exercises, or learn formal algorithms through tools that are not designed as games.
incumbents_and_gap: Logic-grid puzzles and human-sort games teach deduction, but often front-load notation. Word games and coding sites do not turn partial-order discovery into a compact visual game for general players.
smallest_useful_product: A 1–2 player browser deduction race: arrange six eccentric museum exhibits from lightest to heaviest, spending a limited number of comparison tokens; discovered relations animate into a constellation of clues. Solo runs take 5 minutes; two players can share a room code and solve the same case asynchronously. Each case changes objects, hidden ordering graph, and one special inference rule. Non-goals: school dashboards, AI tutoring, long text lessons, and competitive global matchmaking.
success_measure: At least 60% of first-time players solve a beginner case without opening the rules panel, and 20% attempt a second case after seeing their comparison efficiency.
monetization: one-time — a curated case pack is a transparent purchase and avoids education-data or ad incentives.
constraints: Do not claim assessment or educational outcomes without testing; use original cases and accessible shapes/text rather than color alone; room codes must expire.
why_distinct: It makes information-efficient ordering into a readable detective game rather than wrapping a sorting exercise in points.

title: Signal School
user: Curious adults, teams, and older children who learn abstract systems better by negotiating a playful shared problem than by reading a lesson or watching a tutorial.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A programmer/climber describes people understanding avalanche-risk and Unix-pipeline concepts while playing cards in a bar, then asks what makes games effective for abstract technical learning.
A parent working on at-home learning ideas asks the HN community about single-page learning games built for children.

A maintained community recommendation list explicitly filters for games without ads, battle passes, daily-logins, or infinite microtransactions—constraints relevant to a small learning-through-play game.

recurrence: Two 2026 requests independently seek learning through playable, compact formats; one includes a direct observed group-learning outcome. A separate community thread also shows active demand for games that avoid retention-driven monetization.
current_workaround: Use flashcards, worksheets, long tutorial videos, workplace icebreakers, or physical card games that are hard to share remotely.
incumbents_and_gap: Kahoot and quiz platforms center recall; coding tutorials center instruction. Physical teaching card games can create conversation but are not instantly shareable. The gap is a small finished cooperative systems game, not a classroom tool.
smallest_useful_product: A 2–4 player browser signal-routing game: each player sees only one part of a small network and must coordinate three rounds to deliver messages before a storm. Every 12-minute run teaches one transferable systems idea—queues, bottlenecks, redundancy, or feedback—through play, then ends with a one-sentence debrief card. Runs vary in network topology and role assignment. Non-goals: LMS integration, grading, surveillance, content generation, or pretending to certify skills.
success_measure: In moderated playtests, 70% of groups can correctly predict the final bottleneck after a second run, and at least half voluntarily start another topology.
monetization: one-time — a small scenario set can be paid for without selling student data or imposing classroom subscriptions.
constraints: No learner profiles or analytics by default; claims must be framed as game goals, not validated pedagogy; use original examples and permit keyboard-only play.
why_distinct: The learning emerges from asymmetric cooperative play and a real ending, rather than a gamified quiz or a tool marketed to gamers.

title: Roomcode Tactics
user: Two remote friends who want a low-stakes, room-code tactical game that survives a deployment/reconnect and does not demand a persistent account or a huge concurrent community.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer asks how to build a turn-based multiplayer browser game in 2025, specifically concerned that deployments will interrupt ongoing games.
A 2026 itch.io devlog presents a free browser multiplayer sandbox, confirming browser-native multiplayer remains an active indie format rather than an abandoned distribution channel.

recurrence: The HN request exposes the reliability constraint of browser turn-based play; the independent itch.io thread confirms ongoing browser-multiplayer experimentation in 2026.
current_workaround: Use Board Game Arena/Discord/Steam, wait for a friend to install a client, or build a bespoke multiplayer prototype whose sessions break during deployment.
incumbents_and_gap: Board Game Arena has breadth and accounts; online tactics games usually require a client, ladder, or community population. A tiny asynchronous room can avoid matchmaking and still offer meaningful interaction.
smallest_useful_product: A two-player, room-code asynchronous tactics game on a 7×7 map. Each side gets five turns over up to 24 hours, submits a simultaneous move, and receives a short animated resolution; a match ends in 10–15 decisions. Maps rotate through weather and objective rules. Non-goals: real-time combat, public matchmaking, guilds, global ladder, or long-lived worlds.
success_measure: At least 60% of created rooms receive a second player move, 40% complete, and fewer than 2% of completed games require support for an interrupted deployment/reconnect.
monetization: free — room-code sharing needs a zero-friction first match; one-time map-pack support can be tested after completion rates are proven.
constraints: Persist moves and deterministic state before response; use idempotent turn submission and signed opaque room tokens; throttle abuse without forcing accounts; no copyrighted board-game rules or maps.
why_distinct: The design is intentionally a resilient, finite correspondence game—not a live-service tactics clone with matchmaking.
